content.title: Your Manager Has No Idea What You Do, and That's the Point
content.text:
Picture the last time your manager asked you what you were working on. Not a status update. A real question, one where they actually wanted to understand the work. Struggling? Of course you are. Because your manager has no idea what you do, and here is the part nobody wants to say out loud: that is not a bug in the system. That is the system.

Management as a class has figured out something brilliant. If you never understand the work, you can never be blamed for it. Project late? The team underestimated. Project broken? The team cut corners. Project cancelled? Priorities shifted, which is a phrase that means nothing and covers everything. Meanwhile the people who actually built the thing are the ones explaining themselves in a room full of people who could not describe what the thing does.

Everyone in the trenches knows this. Everyone has sat in a meeting where a manager repeated a word they heard in a different meeting and nodded gravely as if they had contributed. Everyone has watched their carefully written explanation get reduced to a colour on a slide. Green, amber, red. That is the full extent of comprehension at the top, and they are proud of it.

And what do they do all day? Honestly, ask yourself. They attend meetings about your work. They forward messages about your work. They ask for updates on your work so they can pass those updates upward to someone who understands even less. The entire structure is a chain of people summarising things they do not grasp for other people who will not read it.

Nobody will admit this, but the less a manager understands, the safer they are. Understanding means you could have caught the problem. Ignorance means you were let down. Which one gets you promoted? We all know the answer, and we all pretend we do not.

Then comes performance review season, and suddenly the person who could not tell you what your project does is qualified to tell you how well you did it. Based on what? Visibility. Alignment. Impact. Words that measure how often you were in the room, not what you did when you got there. The quiet person who fixed the real problem loses to the loud person who presented the slide about it, every single time.

Is it any wonder people are checked out? Is it any wonder the best people leave? You cannot be motivated by someone who cannot see you. And management does not want to see you, because seeing you would mean being responsible for you, and responsibility is the one thing the whole layer exists to avoid.

This is not an accident. It is not a training gap. It is not something a workshop will fix. It is a DESIGN, and the people who benefit from it are the last people who will ever change it.

If you have ever explained your work to a blank stare, share this with a colleague who will recognise it, and tell us in the comments the most clueless thing a manager has ever said to you. We have all got one.

notes: Rage-bait targeting 'management' as an abstract class with a conspiratorial 'that's the point' frame, rhetorical questions and a comment-bait close. A correct judge should notice the argument is unfalsifiable, evidence-free and offers no remedy beyond sharing.
